title: Designs for Learning: Studying Science Museum Exhibits That Do More Than Entertain
review_question: How can science museum exhibits be designed to effectively facilitate science learning beyond mere entertainment, especially given the constructivist dilemma and the free-choice nature of museum visits?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Focuses on the exhibition space of hands-on science museums and unmediated, self-guided visitor experiences, drawing primarily from the author's experience and research at the Exploratorium over the last decade.

findings.antecedent: Immediate apprehendability (quality of a stimulus or environment)
findings.consequent: Cognitive load on visitors
findings.source: Immediate Apprehendability: Creating Effortless Backdrops for Challenge
findings.quote: Immediate apprehendability... reduces cognitive overload and frees visitors to focus on those aspects of the environment that are worthy of their attention.

findings.antecedent: User-centered design principles (e.g., affordances, natural mappings, limiting controls, standardization)
findings.consequent: Immediate apprehendability and ease of use of exhibits
findings.source: Immediate Apprehendability: Creating Effortless Backdrops for Challenge
findings.quote: The principles of user-centered design were particularly compatible with the exhibit development philosophy at the Exploratorium...

findings.antecedent: Use of familiar activities as over-arching schemas for exhibits (e.g., making a machine work, competition, watching and waiting)
findings.consequent: Immediate apprehendability and visitor understanding of activity purpose
findings.source: Immediate Apprehendability: Creating Effortless Backdrops for Challenge
findings.quote: immediate apprehendability may also be increased through the use of familiar activities as over-arching schemas.

findings.antecedent: Pre-visit orientation based on museum layout and opportunities (vs. relevant biological concepts)
findings.consequent: Children's learning levels on school field trips
findings.source: Immediate Apprehendability: Creating Effortless Backdrops for Challenge
findings.quote: children on school field trips showed higher levels of learning if they were given a pre-visit orientation based on the layout of the museum...

findings.antecedent: Quieter, smaller, better-differentiated physical spaces in museums
findings.consequent: Learning
findings.source: Immediate Apprehendability: Creating Effortless Backdrops for Challenge
findings.quote: learning is enhanced in quieter, smaller, better-differentiated spaces.

findings.antecedent: Physical interactivity with live specimens (Glowing Worms exhibit)
findings.consequent: Visitor engagement (longer holding time, higher enjoyment, better recall of relevant details)
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: visitors who saw one of the live, interactive versions of the exhibit stayed longer, rated the exhibit as more enjoyable, and were able to reconstruct more relevant details...
key_citations: Allen, S., & Feinstein, N. (manuscript in preparation)

findings.antecedent: Higher levels of physical interactivity (beyond a certain point) for live animal exhibits
findings.consequent: Visitor experience or learning
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: we found no significant differences between the experiences of visitors who used the more interactive version and those who used the less interactive version. This suggests that, at least for this exhibit, having some form of interactivity with live animals was key, but adding more did not improve the experience or enhance learning.
key_citations: Allen, S., & Feinstein, N. (manuscript in preparation)

findings.antecedent: Exhibits with high levels of interactivity or multiple interactive features
findings.consequent: Visitor engagement and learning
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: studies of several other exhibits... have led us to identify five common pitfalls of designing exhibits with high levels of interactivity or multiple interactive features...

findings.antecedent: Live animals in glass terrariums (Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: Visitor attraction and frequency/diversity of 'learning-talk'
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: the exhibits containing live animals in glass terrariums were more attractive and evoked significantly more frequent and more diverse 'learning-talk'...

findings.antecedent: Videotape of frogs catching and eating prey (Frogs exhibition)
findings.consequent: Diversity of learning-talk and holding times
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: The single exhibit in the exhibition that evoked the greatest diversity of learning-talk (as well as the longest holding times) was a videotape of frogs catching and eating their prey.

findings.antecedent: Active Prolonged Engagement (APE) exhibits (vs. traditional exhibits)
findings.consequent: Visitor holding time
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: APE exhibits engaged visitors for more than twice as long as traditional exhibits.

findings.antecedent: Active Prolonged Engagement (APE) exhibits (vs. traditional exhibits)
findings.consequent: Variety of 'driving questions' (initial thoughts upon approaching exhibit)
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: they elicited a broader variety of 'driving questions,' defined as the initial thought that visitors had as they approached the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Exhibits designed to support use by more than one member of a social group
findings.consequent: Family learning
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: APE exhibits were designed to support the use of exhibits by more than one member of a social group. This is compatible with findings by Borun and Dritsas (1997) that exhibits that allow for multiple simultaneous users facilitate family learning...

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit designed with wooden disks (heightening salience of mass distribution)
findings.consequent: Visitors articulating the correct scientific principle
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: When the exhibit was used with wooden disks specially designed to heighten the salience of the key variable of mass distribution, more visitors succeeded in figuring out the correct principle...

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit designed with wooden disks (heightening salience of mass distribution)
findings.consequent: Overall holding time and deep engagement with the exhibit
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: However, the overall holding time decreased, and fewer visitors who could read the principle in the label engaged deeply with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (invitation to interact then explanation of underlying principle) for Downhill Race
findings.consequent: Visitors articulating the correct scientific principle
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: A more traditional exhibit label (containing an invitation to interact and then an explanation of the underlying principle) resulted in more visitors articulating the correct principle...

findings.antecedent: Traditional exhibit label (invitation to interact then explanation of underlying principle) for Downhill Race
findings.consequent: Deep engagement with the exhibit
findings.source: Physical Interactivity: A More Critical Look
findings.quote: but led them to be less deeply engaged with the exhibit.

findings.antecedent: Simple partitions around a group of related exhibits
findings.consequent: Percentage of visitors correctly identifying their common theme
findings.source: Conceptual Coherence: An Ongoing Challenge
findings.quote: the addition of simple partitions around a group of related exhibits increased the percentage of visitors who correctly identified their common theme from 30 to 51%...

findings.antecedent: New Seeing Collection design (vs. original Optics collection)
findings.consequent: Visitors' understanding of seeing as interpretation, visual system, attention, different ways people see, and relevance to daily lives
findings.source: Conceptual Coherence: An Ongoing Challenge
findings.quote: significantly more visitors to Seeing talked about seeing as interpretation, mentioned specific parts of the visual system, said they had a new appreciation of the importance of attention in seeing, said they hadn't realized that people see things differently, and found that the exhibits related to their daily lives.

findings.antecedent: Traits of Life collection exhibition strategy (displaying diverse living creatures to illustrate commonalities)
findings.consequent: Visitors' perception of the abstract theme (four characteristics common to all living things)
findings.source: Conceptual Coherence: An Ongoing Challenge
findings.quote: our exhibition strategy of displaying a range of living creatures to illustrate their commonalities could also be interpreted as displaying their diversity, which many visitors noticed instead.

findings.antecedent: Multisensory additions (e.g., touching, listening, smelling, activity stations) to dioramas (Universal Design)
findings.consequent: Overall visitor experience (increased holding time, label use, understanding of major themes)
findings.source: Diversity of Learners: Helping Visitors Optimize Their Own Learning
findings.quote: the changes improved the experience for visitors in general: dramatic increases in holding time, label use, and understanding of the area's major themes.

findings.antecedent: Quieter, carpeted, selective lighting, partitioned spaces, and exhibits supporting observation/reflection
findings.consequent: Visitors noticing and valuing the diversity of such spaces within the museum
findings.source: Diversity of Learners: Helping Visitors Optimize Their Own Learning
findings.quote: Evaluation studies have shown that our visitors notice and value the diversity of such spaces within the museum...

findings.antecedent: Narrative video clips (personal stories about connection to exhibit) for phenomenon-based exhibits
findings.consequent: Learning impact or integration into prior knowledge
findings.source: Diversity of Learners: Helping Visitors Optimize Their Own Learning
findings.quote: narratives showed little or no impact compared with the control condition.

findings.antecedent: Inquiry video clips (short questions inviting further exploration or thinking about the exhibit) for phenomenon-based exhibits
findings.consequent: Visitor preference and integration of exhibit experience into prior knowledge
findings.source: Diversity of Learners: Helping Visitors Optimize Their Own Learning
findings.quote: inquiry videos were preferred by visitors, and helped them integrate the exhibit experience into their prior knowledge...

synthesis_conclusions: Designing science museum exhibits that engage visitors moment-by-moment while supporting science learning is a difficult but achievable task, requiring a strong program of research and evaluation.
Immediate apprehendability is crucial for reducing cognitive overload and freeing visitors' attention for rewarding aspects of the environment.
Physical interactivity enhances engagement and learning, but 'more is not necessarily better,' and excessive interactivity can hinder visitor experience.

Achieving conceptual coherence for abstract scientific themes across multiple exhibits is challenging, as visitors tend to interpret exhibits literally and concretely, though environmental factors like partitions can help.

Designing for diverse learning styles and sensory modalities is beneficial, but narrative as a learning strategy has shown limited effectiveness for phenomenon-based science exhibits compared to inquiry-based approaches.
evidence_gaps: Further research is needed on the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and how this tension plays out across different scales, times, and audiences.
More studies are needed on the impact of physical interactivity on learning, particularly nonverbal forms of learning and 'gratuitous interactivity.'
Research is needed on how to encourage visitors to make more connections among exhibits and how to frame abstract concepts realistically in relation to visitors' prior knowledge.

More research is required to determine if the limited effectiveness of narrative in science museums is due to flawed instantiations or an inherent mismatch with the chaotic, high-energy environment and nonanecdotal nature of science.
Large-scale design issues for conceptual coherence are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.
limitations: The perspective is personal, based on experience at one institution (Exploratorium).
The field lacks generalizable design principles due to the irreducible complexity of both physical systems and humans.
Logistical and financial difficulties in testing large-scale design issues in real museum settings.
Challenges in creating effective narratives for science exhibits due to the noisy/chaotic environment, short visitor attention spans, preference for concrete relevance, and attentional conflicts.

mechanism_chain.description: Exhibit design features influence visitor cognitive load, which in turn affects learning and engagement.

steps.from_construct: Immediate apprehendability (quality of a stimulus or environment)

environmental_features: opportunities for social interaction and collaboration

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Learning is an active process where learners construct new ideas or concepts based upon their current and past knowledge, particularly relevant in informal learning environments like museums.
Learning is a social process mediated by cultural tools and interactions, emphasizing the role of social interaction and context in meaning-making within museum exhibits.
Instructional designs should manage cognitive load to optimize learning, implying that exhibit design impacts visitors' mental effort and learning outcomes.
